item.title: Cross-Platform Process Containment: Job Objects vs Process Groups vs cgroups
item.description: Every turn a shipmates crew member takes is a subprocess: claude or the codex app-server, which in turn spawns shells, go test, npm, whatever the task calls for. Two things have to be true about that tree. When a turn ends or gets killed, the whole tree goes, including the grandchildren. And if somebody sets a memory or CPU budget, the budget applies to the whole tree, not just the process I happened to start.

item.title: Bind Mounts Across Mount Namespaces: Four PRs and a Container Escape
item.description: GitHub Actions has a container: key that runs a job’s steps inside an image of your choosing. It’s popular because it gives you a reproducible toolchain without building a custom runner image. On a self-hosted runner it works by having the runner drive Docker, and on ephemerd “Docker” is a shim that speaks the Docker API and creates containers in containerd. Getting bind mounts right through that shim took four PRs in a week. A couple of months later the version that worked turned out to be an escape.

item.title: Zero-Dependency Deployments - Single Binary for WordPress
item.description: The standard way to run a WordPress site is four services: nginx for HTTP and TLS, php-fpm to run PHP, MySQL for data, and Redis once the site gets slow enough that someone installs an object cache plugin. That’s four processes, four config files, three sockets between them, and four things to upgrade. For a big site that’s fine. For a brochure site, a staging copy, a PR preview, a CI job that needs a real WordPress to test a plugin against, or a box at the edge, it’s absurd.

item.title: Kata Containers for CI: Boot Cost Isn't the Problem, File I/O Is
item.description: Of the three platforms ephemerd runs jobs on, Linux has the weakest isolation. Windows jobs get a Hyper-V isolated container with its own kernel, macOS jobs get a whole VM, and a Linux job is an ordinary runc container sharing the host kernel. A kernel escape from a Linux job is a host compromise. Kata Containers fixes that by putting each container in a lightweight VM with its own kernel, and it plugs into containerd as just another runtime handler. So I added it in #155, measured it, and left it off by default. This post is why.

item.title: Per-Tenant Network Policy in One Process: ePHPm's eBPF Thread Tags
item.description:
In multi-tenant mode ePHPm serves every site in sites_dir from one process. Every tenant’s PHP runs as the same OS user, on the same pool of ZTS threads, and a thread that just served blog.example will serve shop.example a few milliseconds later. That’s the density win. It also means the kernel has no idea which tenant is behind a given connect(). As far as Linux is concerned it’s all ephpm-web.

Most of the isolation work in ePHPm happens above the kernel: open_basedir, the function denylist, per-site databases and KV keyspaces. Network is the one place where that isn’t enough. This week we brought eBPF in to give the kernel a per-tenant identity. It went from a roadmap doc on Wednesday morning to merged that evening (#413, aimed at v0.8.1). v0.8.1 never got a release because its Linux legs failed to link. v0.8.2 shipped with the BPF object silently stubbed out, and v0.8.3 was the first release that actually carried it. This post covers what it enforces, what it costs, what broke on the way out the door, and what it doesn’t do.

item.title: My iptables Rule Matched 0 Packets in 9.8 GB
item.description:
After a week of Windows firewall rules that listed fine and enforced nothing, I went back to the Linux side of ephemerd feeling pretty good about it. iptables is the boring, well-understood one. item.title: ephemerd: One Daemon, a Fresh Runner Per Job, Every OS
item.description: I have CI that needs Linux amd64, Linux arm64, Windows and macOS, and GitHub-hosted runners for all four get expensive fast, especially the arm64 and Mac minutes. Self-hosted runners fix the bill and create a different problem. A stock actions/runner on a box you own runs whatever the workflow says, keeps whatever the last job left behind, and is one fork PR away from somebody running code on your LAN.
